paper_metadata.title: Quantum Attacks on Bitcoin, and How to Protect Against Them

summary: The paper is a theoretical resource-estimation study of quantum attacks on Bitcoin. It estimates Grover-based proof-of-work mining at 2402 logical qubits and 474168 T gates per oracle call, with an example 4.4×10^6 physical-qubit implementation at D=10^12 and pg=5×10^-4, while Shor-based ECDSA breaking uses 2334 logical qubits and 1.28×10^11 Toffoli gates for n=256. It also shows Momentum-style proof-of-work is more quantum resistant, with quantum runtime lower bounded by T^(2/3) rather than Grover's T^(1/2).

experiments.description: Theoretical Grover-search attack on Bitcoin proof-of-work (Hashcash/SHA256d) with resource estimates under surface-code error correction and superconducting gate speeds.

algorithm.variant: Grover search for valid Bitcoin block header / proof-of-work

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Search over well-formed Bitcoin block headers by varying nonce, transactions, and timestamp bits; Grover oracle marks headers whose double-SHA256 hash is below target t.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Find header such that h(header) ≤ t, where h = SHA256(SHA256(header)).
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Oracle predicate encodes the proof-of-work threshold; no additional penalty terms.

problem_instance.description: Bitcoin proof-of-work mining / hashcash attack analysis.

dataset_specification.description: Uses blockchain.info hash-rate and difficulty observations; example difficulty D = 860×10^9 in 2017 and projected future difficulty curves.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Theoretical random-oracle model; difficulty extrapolated from historical Bitcoin network hash-rate data.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Analytical resource estimation and projected crossover analysis; no empirical runs reported.

noise_model.noise_type: physical gate errors with surface-code fault tolerance

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: None beyond theoretical construction of a deterministic mapping g from bitstrings to well-formed block headers.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Measure candidate header and verify hash condition classically.
implementation_details.total_execution_time: Analytical; examples include effective hash rate 13.8 GH/s at 66.7 MHz and 2.0×10^3 TH/s at 50 GHz under optimistic assumptions.

results.unit: clock cycles per logical T gate

speedup_claims.conditions: random oracle model; fault-tolerant surface-code quantum computer; effective rate depends on gate speed and error correction overhead
speedup_claims.caveats: Near-term quantum devices are slower in wall-clock terms than ASIC miners; paper states no advantage at current difficulty and hardware assumptions.

speedup_claims.conditions: if quantum gate speeds reach 100 GHz
speedup_claims.caveats: Described as unlikely in the next decade.

speedup_claims.factor: 2.56x * sqrt(d) for d parallel quantum processors
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a parallelization scaling law, not a classical-vs-quantum advantage.

speedup_claims.factor: no advantage / slower than ASICs at current parameters
speedup_claims.caveats: Effective hash rate 13.8 GH/s vs 14 TH/s ASIC example.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(sqrt(N)) oracle queries for unstructured search; effective hash rate scales as O(sqrt(D)) under the paper's model.
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(N) hash evaluations; expected hashes proportional to 2^256/t = D×2^32.
complexity_analysis.constant_factor_quantum: π/4 with additional surface-code and T-gate overheads; effective hash rate h_QC = 0.28*s/sqrt(D)/c_tau.
complexity_analysis.constant_factor_classical: 1 hash per verification; ASIC example 14 TH/s cited.
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: Not explicitly given; paper states current ASICs outperform near-term quantum devices and that quantum advantage may not appear in the next decade.
complexity_analysis.wall_clock_quantum: Example: 13.8 GH/s at 66.7 MHz, pg=5e-4, D=1e12; 2.0×10^3 TH/s at 50 GHz under optimistic assumptions.
complexity_analysis.wall_clock_classical: Example ASIC hash rate 14 TH/s cited.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established; paper gives only asymptotic Grover scaling and example resource estimates, not a demonstrated crossover problem size.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Example resource estimate: 2402 logical qubits, 474168 T gates per oracle call, about 4.4×10^6 physical qubits at D=10^12, pg=5×10^-4, and 66.7 MHz; optimistic 50 GHz case gives 2.0×10^3 TH/s effective hash rate.
limiting_factors: Slow logical gate speed relative to ASICs

notes: This is a theoretical resource-estimation study, not an executed hardware experiment.
num_qubits refers to logical qubits for the Grover attack; physical qubits are separately estimated as 4.4×10^6 in one example.
The paper explicitly states the quantum computer is more than one thousand times slower than off-the-shelf ASICs in the cited example.
This is a theoretical resource-estimation study, not an executed experiment.

experiments.description: Theoretical Shor-based attack on Bitcoin ECDSA signatures (secp256k1) with surface-code resource estimates and superconducting gate-speed projections.

algorithm.variant: Shor algorithm for elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem (ECDLP)

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Quantum algorithm for ECDLP on the secp256k1 elliptic curve; public key revealed from a Bitcoin transaction is the input.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Recover private key m from public key relation on elliptic curve (discrete logarithm).
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: No penalty formulation; algorithmic reduction via Shor's period-finding/discrete-log procedure.

problem_instance.description: Bitcoin ECDSA signature attack on broadcast or reused public keys.

dataset_specification.description: Bitcoin uses ECDSA over secp256k1; attack window is from public-key broadcast until transaction confirmation.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Theoretical analysis only; no dataset preprocessing.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Analytical resource estimation; example runtimes reported for selected clock speeds and error rates.

noise_model.noise_type: physical gate errors with surface-code fault tolerance

implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Measure candidate key and verify against public key / signature relation.
implementation_details.total_execution_time: Example: 6.49 days at 66.6 MHz and pg=5e-4; 30 minutes at 10 GHz and pg=1e-5.

speedup_claims.conditions: Shor algorithm on a fault-tolerant universal quantum computer
speedup_claims.caveats: Paper does not give an explicit classical asymptotic bound, only states the problem is believed hard classically.

speedup_claims.factor: breaks signature scheme in less than 10 minutes
speedup_claims.baseline_method: Bitcoin block interval / transaction confirmation window
speedup_claims.conditions: as early as 2027 under optimistic hardware projections
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a forecast, not an experimental demonstration.

speedup_claims.baseline_method: same quantum attack under improved hardware
speedup_claims.conditions: clock speed increases from 66.6 MHz to 10 GHz and physical gate error rate improves from 5e-4 to 1e-5

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Polynomial-time quantum algorithm for ECDLP; gate count scales as O(n^3).
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Believed hard classically; no explicit asymptotic classical bound stated in the paper.
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: Not explicitly given; paper states attack could be feasible as early as 2027 under optimistic assumptions.
complexity_analysis.wall_clock_quantum: 6.49 days at 66.6 MHz, pg=5e-4; 30 minutes at 10 GHz, pg=1e-5.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established; the paper gives only resource estimates for n=256 and does not identify a practical crossover size.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Example resource estimate: 2334 logical qubits, 1.28×10^11 Toffoli gates, 1.7×10^6 physical qubits at pg=5×10^-4 and 66.6 MHz; 30 minutes at 10 GHz and pg=10^-5 in the optimistic case.
limiting_factors: Requires sufficiently large universal quantum computer

experiments.description: Theoretical analysis of a Momentum-style memory-hard proof-of-work using collision finding, comparing classical and quantum query complexity; no hardware execution.

algorithm.variant: Quantum search over Momentum proof-of-work candidates with collision-finding subroutine

hyperparameters.condition: find H,a,b such that h1(H∥a∥b) ≤ t and h2(H∥a)=h2(H∥b)

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Search over header H and nonce-like values a,b; collision condition on h2 plus threshold condition on h1.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Find H,a,b satisfying both a hash threshold and a collision predicate.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Collision predicate and threshold condition jointly define feasibility; no penalty terms.

problem_instance.description: Alternative proof-of-work (Momentum) for blockchain security analysis.

dataset_specification.description: Abstract hash functions h1:{0,1}*→{0,1}^n and h2:{0,1}*→{0,1}^ℓ; no concrete dataset.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Analytical comparison of asymptotic running times; no empirical runs.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: None; theoretical derivation of optimal subset size and collision search cost.

speedup_claims.factor: no quadratic speedup; fastest quantum algorithm is at least T^(2/3)
speedup_claims.baseline_method: optimal classical algorithm with runtime T
speedup_claims.conditions: Momentum-style proof-of-work with non-constant subset size S
speedup_claims.caveats: Paper states quantum computer would not achieve quadratic advantage once S is more than constant size.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: At least T^(2/3) for the fastest quantum algorithm under the paper's analysis; collision testing requires |S|^(2/3) and Grover over H adds sqrt(m).
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: T for the optimal classical algorithm, where T = sqrt(2^(n+ℓ)/t).
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: Not applicable; paper states quantum computer would not achieve quadratic advantage once S is more than constant size.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not applicable as a practical advantage claim; the paper's point is that the quantum algorithm is only T^(2/3), not quadratically faster than the best classical strategy.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: No concrete hardware resource estimate is given; the paper only provides asymptotic lower bounds and compares T^(2/3) quantum scaling against T classical scaling.
limiting_factors: Grover over H still leaves subquadratic but not quadratic improvement

notes: This section is purely theoretical and does not specify a concrete gate-based circuit resource count or hardware platform.
The paper's conclusion is comparative and theoretical: Momentum reduces quantum advantage relative to Bitcoin PoW.

experiments.description: Alternative proof-of-work analysis for Momentum showing that a quantum computer cannot obtain a quadratic advantage once collision-finding is required.

algorithm.variant: Momentum proof-of-work with collision finding and Grover search over H

key_results: Classical running time is minimized at T = sqrt(2^(n+ℓ)/t) for |S| = sqrt(2^(n+ℓ)/t).
Quantum running time is lower bounded by sqrt(m)|S|^(2/3), so the best quantum algorithm is at least T^(2/3), not T^(1/2).
The paper concludes this Momentum-style proof-of-work is more quantum resistant than Bitcoin's current hashcash PoW.
